'''Jean Marcel Rouxel''' (February 24, 1935 in [[Malestroit]] – March 19, 1998 in [[Nantes]]) was a French synthetic chemist known for his work in [[Solid-state chemistry|solid state synthesis]] of low-dimensional materials.<ref name=Nature /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jean Rouxel's research between chemistry and physics - p27 - N°231 - L'Actualité Chimique, le journal de la SCF |url=https://new.societechimiquedefrance.fr/numero/jean-rouxels-research-between-chemistry-and-physics-p27-n231/ |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=Société Chimique de France (SCF) |language=fr-FR}}</ref><ref name=CM>{{Cite journal |date=1998-10-01 |title=Jean Rouxel 1935−1998 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/cm9810032 |journal=Chemistry of Materials |language=en |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=4–5 |doi=10.1021/cm9810032 |issn=0897-4756|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He pioneered the use of solid [[Precursor (chemistry)|precursors]] in [[soft chemistry]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Tarascon |first=Jean-Marie |title=Chemistry of Materials and Energy. Examples and Future of a Millennial Science : Inaugural Lecture |date=2017-02-23 |url=http://books.openedition.org/cdf/4852 |series=Leçons inaugurales |place=Paris |publisher=Collège de France |isbn=978-2-7226-0461-2 |access-date=2022-06-09}}</ref><ref name=precursor />

== Education and career ==
Rouxel studied at the [[University of Rennes]] and the [[University of Bordeaux]], where he received his PhD in 1961 under [[Paul Hagenmuller]] on two classes of aluminum compounds. After that he was an assistant in Bordeaux and after military service in [[Algeria]] between 1962 and 1963, he went to the newly founded laboratory for solid state chemistry (today named after him) at the [[University of Nantes]]. There he became an assistant professor in 1964 and a professor in 1968. From 1986 to 1998 he was scientific advisor at [[Rhône-Poulenc]]. In 1988 he became director of the Institute for Materials (Institut des Matériaux, which arose from the Institute for Solid State Chemistry) in Nantes, which he remained until his death in 1998. From 1991 to 1996, he was a professor at the [[Institut Universitaire de France]]. From 1994 to 1995, he was a professor at the [[École normale supérieure de Lyon]] and from 1997 until his death he was a professor of solid state chemistry at the [[Collège de France]].<ref name=Nature>{{Cite journal |last=Pouchard |first=Michel |date=1998 |title=Jean Rouxel (1935-98) |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=393 |issue=6682 |pages=218 |doi=10.1038/30367 |s2cid=205000450 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free }}</ref>

He synthesized and characterized numerous solids in low dimensions (that is, one or two dimensions) and explored the properties of one-dimensional inorganic chains, such as the phase transition to charge density waves. Another area of research was incommensurable structures in solids and the connection between chemistry and electronic band structure in solids. He studied the mechanisms of anionic polymerization in solids and the competition of anions and cations in [[redox reactions]] in solids. He is also working on a type of synthesis based on biological processes, which is called [[soft chemistry]] (''chimie douce'' in French), after a word coined by the French chemist [[Jacques Livage]] in 1977.<ref name=Nature /><ref name=precursor>{{Cite journal |last=Rouxel |first=J |date=1996 |title=Chimie douce with solid precursors, past and present |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0167273896000197 |journal=Solid State Ionics |language=en |volume=84 |issue=3–4 |pages=141–149 |doi=10.1016/0167-2738(96)00019-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
In 1974 he received the [[CNRS Silver Medal]] and in 1997 the [[CNRS Gold Medal]] and the Prix Paul Pascal from the [[French Academy of Sciences]]. In 1992 he was awarded the [[Gay-Lussac Humboldt Prize]]. Rouxel received the [[Alexander von Humboldt Research Award]] (1993) and gave the Debye Lecture of the [[Cornell University]] section of the [[American Chemical Society]]. He was [[Knight of the Legion of Honor]] (1988, officer from 1997) and officer of the [[Ordre national du Mérite]] and commander of the [[Palmes académiques]]. In 1988 he became a member of the [[Académie des sciences]] and he was a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1992), the [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] (1997) and the [[Indian Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jean Rouxel, a memory - p24 - N°231 - L'Actualité Chimique, le journal de la SCF |url=https://new.societechimiquedefrance.fr/numero/jean-rouxel-a-memory-p24-n231/ |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=Société Chimique de France (SCF) |language=fr-FR}}</ref><ref name=CM />

== Personal life ==
Rouxel had two sons and three daughters with his wife Yannick. He died from ruptured [[aneurysm]].<ref name=CM />
